variants.note: old-fashioned; some speakers, especially in Irish English and parts of the American South, add a light puff of breath before the **w**

pronunciation.notes: The **wh** is said like a plain **w**, so **when** sounds like **wen**.

core_idea: **When** most often says at what time something happens; less often it shows that something is a surprising or odd thing to do.

senses.definition: at the time that something happens or happened
senses.explanation: A **when** clause names the time of the action in the main clause. It can come first, with a comma after it (*When the phone rang, she was in the shower*), or after the main clause, with no comma (*She was in the shower when the phone rang*). In a clause about the future, **when** normally takes the present tense, not **will**: *I will call you when I arrive*, not *when I will arrive*.

examples.text: Call me when you get home.
When I was a child, we lived by the sea.
She was reading when the phone rang.
I'll tell you when I know more.

compare.note: **while** points to a period of time during which something happens; **when** can point to a single point or a period
**whenever** means any time that, not one particular time

subsenses.explanation: **When** can describe a habit or a rule as well as a single event.

examples.text: When it rains, this road floods.
The dog barks when someone knocks on the door.

adaptation.semantic: Some languages use one word for both **when** (a point in time) and **if** (a condition). English keeps them apart: *when you arrive* assumes it will happen; *if you arrive* does not.
adaptation.grammar: In a clause about future time, **when** is normally followed by the present tense, not **will**: *when she arrives*, not *when she will arrive*. **Will** can appear here only to show willingness or insistence.

senses.definition: although it seems strange or unnecessary that
senses.explanation: Used to show surprise or mild criticism: the main clause says or asks why the action in the **when** clause seems wrong or pointless. It often follows a question with **why**.

examples.text: Why walk when you can drive?
She always takes the bus when she could easily walk.
He gave up when he was so close to finishing.

compare.note: **although** is the more general word for a surprising contrast; **when** is used this way mainly after a question with **why** or a criticism

adaptation.semantic: This contrastive use of **when** often needs a word meaning **although** or **since** in another language, not that language's usual word for time.

examples.text: When it comes to cooking, Sam is the expert.
I'm not very patient when it comes to waiting in line.

learner_errors.incorrect: I will call you when I will arrive.
learner_errors.correct: I will call you when I arrive.
learner_errors.note: A **when** clause about the future normally uses the present tense, not **will**.

learner_errors.incorrect: When you will need help, tell me.
learner_errors.correct: When you need help, tell me.
learner_errors.note: **Will** does not normally follow **when** in a clause about the future, except to show willingness (*when you will just listen, I'll explain*).

see_also.note: the question word **when** (*When did you arrive?*)
